sentences.text: The largest known skull of Purussaurus measures up to 1.4 meters from the snout tip to the quadrates. Its teeth were consistently around 50 mm long and curved slightly backwards across all three species. These teeth were taller and more pointed at the front, while being lower and more rounded at the back. The teeth of this genus are curved slightly backward, pointing toward the inside of the mouth.
The Venezuelan species possessed a flattened skull much more than the other two species.

Purussaurus had all sense organs at the top of its head, indicating it was an ambush predator similar to modern caimans. Its large body size and wide skull suggest a lifestyle that was mostly aquatic.

Some paleontologists estimate the full body length of P. brasiliensis was between 11 and 13 meters, making Purussaurus one of the largest known crocodiles. Some estimates suggest P. brasiliensis might be the largest crocodyliform to have ever existed.

A 2015 study estimated the bite force of Purussaurus at around 69,000 Newtons, or approximately 7 metric tons-force. Purussaurus was perhaps capable of overpowering even the large mammals of its time.

The genus Purussaurus was first described by Rodrigues in 1892. The type species, P. brasiliensis, was described by Barbosa-Rodrigues in 1892. The type species, Purussaurus brasiliensis, was first described in 1892.
New Purussaurus fossils were found in the Peruvian Amazon in 2005 by the Franco-Peruvian Fitzcarrald expedition.

Purussaurus was an apex predator capable of hunting a wide range of prey due to its large size and strength. Adult Purussaurus preyed on large vertebrates like xenarthrans, notoungulates, and giant turtles, facing little competition from smaller carnivores.

Ridges on Purussaurus teeth indicate it hunted large vertebrates by puncturing and holding flesh. Biomechanical models indicate Purussaurus could perform the 'death roll' maneuver to subdue and dismember prey. Biomechanical analyses of skulls indicate that Purussaurus and Deinosuchus may have been capable of performing the "death roll" maneuver.
Purussaurus likely ate Stupendemys turtles, various crocodilians, birds, and mammals including sloths, bats, capybara-like rodents up to 700 kg, primates, and river dolphins.
Bite marks on a phorusrhacid tibia suggest it may have been killed by a young Purussaurus, though whether this was scavenging or active predation is debated.
Researchers suggest that Purussaurus's large size may have made it vulnerable to environmental changes, favoring smaller, more resilient species.

Purussaurus is classified within the family Alligatoridae. Purussaurus belongs to the subfamily Caimaninae. Purussaurus has two direct parent taxa in its classification hierarchy. Purussaurus is currently classified as a giant representative of the subfamily Caimaninae.

Some studies suggest Purussaurus may have been heavier than Sarcosuchus or Deinosuchus due to its broader snout requiring a stronger neck. It is debated whether additional traces on bones of Xenastrapotherium kraglievichi represent scavenging by a crocodyliform similar to Langstonia.
